4     Experience with Design Patterns
We have applied design patterns to the design and construction of a eeveral
systems. We briefly desc.ribe two of theee systema and our experience.

4.1   ET++SwapsManager
The ET++SwapeManager [10] is a highly interactive tool that leta traders value,
price, and perform what-if analyses for a financial instrument called a swap. Dur-
ing this project the developers had to first learn the ET++ due library, then
implement the tool, and finally design a framework for creating "calculation
engines" for different financial instruments. While teaching ET++ we empha-
siled not only learning the clue library but also describing the applied design
patterns. We noticed that design patterns reduced the effort required to learn
ET++. Patterns al80 proved helpful during development in design and code
reviews. Patterll8 provided a common vocabulary to discuaa a design. When-
ever we encountered problems in the design, patterns helped us explore design
alternatives and find solutions.

4.2   QOCA: A Constraint Solving Toolkit
QOCA (Quadratic Optimization Constraint Architecture) [14, 15] is a new
object-oriented constraint-solving toolkit developed at IBM Research. QOCA
leverages recent results in symbolic computation and geometry to support effi-
cient incremental and interactive cOll8traint manipulation. QOCA's architecture
is designed to be flexible. It permits experimentation with different classes of
constraints and domains (e.g., reals, booleans, etc.), different constraint-solving
algorithms for these domains, and different representations (doubles, infinite pre-
cision) for objects in theee domains. QOCA's object-oriented design allows parts
of the system to be varied independently of others. This fiexibility was achieved,
for example, by using Strategy patterns to factor out constraint solving algo-
rithms and Bridges to factor out domains and representations of variables. In
addition, the Observable pattern is used to propagate notifications when vari-
ables change their values.

4.3   Sum.rnary of Observations

The following points summarize the major observations we have made while
applying design patterns:
 - Design patterns motivate developers to go beyond concrete objects; that is,
   they objectify concepts that are not immediately apparent as objects in the
   problem domain.
 - Choosing intuitive class names is important but also difficult. We have found
   that design patterns can help name classes. In the ET++SwapsManager's
   calculation engine framework we encoded the name of the design pattern
712       Erich Gamma

         in the clue name (for example CalculationStrategy or TableAdaptor). This
         convention resulta in longer clue names, but it gives clienta of these c:l&ases
         a hint about their p~.
       - We often apply design patterns "ft.f' the firat implementation of an archi-
         tecture to improve ita design. For example, it it easier to apply the Strategy
         pattern after the initial implementation to create objecb for more .betract
         notiona1ike a calculation engine or cOl1ltraint solver. Patterns were also used
         u tuleta for cluI re£actorinp. We often find ounelves saying, "Make this
         part of a clue into a Strategy," or, "Let'. split the implementation portion
         of this cluI into aBridge."
       - Presenting design patterl1l together with examples of their application
         turned out to be an effective way to teach objec~riented design by example.
       - An important issue with any reuse technology is how a reusable component
         can be adapted to create a problem-apecific component. Design paUerI1I are
         particularly suited to reuse because they are abetract. Though a concrete
         claae structure may not be reuaable, the design pattern underlying it often
         is.
       - Design patterns also reduce the effort required to learn a clue library. Each
         class library has a certain design "culture" characterised by the set of pat-
         terl1l used implicitly by its developers. A specific design pattern is typically
         reused in different places in the library. A client should therefore learn these
         patterns as a first step in learning the library. Once they are familiar with
         the patteroa, they can reuse this understanding. Moreover, bee.oae some
         patterns appear in other class libraries, it is possible to reoae the knowledge
         about patterns when learning other libraries as well.


      5   Related Work
      Design patterns are an approach to software reuse. Krueger [20] introduces the
      following taxonomy to characterize different reuse approaches: software com-
      ponent reuse, software schemM, application generators, transformation systems,
      and software architectures. Design patterns are related to both software schemaa
      and reusable software architectures. Software schemas emphasize reusing ab-
      stract algorithms and data structures. These abstractions are represented for-
      mally so they can be inBtantiated automatically. The Paris system [18] is repre-
      sentative of schema technology. Design patterns are higher-level than schemas;
      they focus on design structures at the level of collaborating classes and not at
      the algorithmic level. In addition, design patterns are not formal descriptions
      and caDDot be instantiated directly. We therefore prefer to view design patterns
      as reusable software architectures. However, the examples Krueger lists in this
      category (blackboard architectures for expert systems, adaptable database sub-
      systems) are all coarse-grained architectures. Design patterns are finer-grained
      and therefore can be characterized as reusable micr~architectures.
          Most research into patterns in the software engineering community has been
      geared towards building knowledge-baaed assistants for automating the appli-
                                                    Original Histonc Documents     71 3

cation of paUema for synthesis (that is, to write programs) and analysis (in
debugging, for example) [13, 24]. The major difference between our work and
that of the knowledge-baaed auiatant community is that design patterns encode
higher-level expertise. Their work has tended to focus on patterns like enumer-
ation and selection, which can be expressed directly as reusable components
in meet exiating object-oriented languages. We believe that characterising and
cataloging higher-level patteme that designers already use informally has an
immediate benefit in teacbing and communicating designs.
    A common approach for reusing object-oriented software architectures are
object-oriented frameworks [32]. A framework is a codified architecture for a
problem domain that can be adapted to solve specific problems. A framework
makes it pOl8ible to reuse an architecture together with a partial concrete im-
plementation. In contrast to frameworks, design patterns allow only the reuse
of abstract micro-architectures without a concrete implementation. However,
design patterns can help define and develop frameworks. Mature frameworks
usually reuse several design patterns. An important distinction between frame-
works and design patterns is that frameworks are implemented in a programming
language. Our patterns are ways of 1Uing a programming language. In this sense
frameworks are more concrete than design patterns.
    Design paUeme are also related to the idioms introduced by Coplien [7].
These idioms are concrete design solutions in the context of C++. Coplien "fo-
cuses on idioms that make C++ programs more expressive." In contrast, design
patterns are more abstract and higher-level than idioms. Patterns try to ab-
stract design rather than programming techniques. Moreover, design patterns
are usually independent of the implementation language.
    There has been interest recently within the object-oriented community [8] in
pattern languages for the architecture of buildings and communities as advocated
by Christopher Alexander in The Timele .. Way of Building [2]. Alexander's
patterna consist of three parts:
 - A context that describes when a pattern is applicable.
 - The problem (or "system of conflicting forces") that the pattern resolves in
   that context.
 - A configuration that describes physical relationships that solve the problem.
Both design patterns and Alexander's patterns share the notion of con-
text/problem/configuration, but our patterns currently do not form a complete
system of patterns and so do not strictly define a pattern language. This may
be because object-oriented design is still a young technology-we may not have
had enough experience in what constitutes good design to extract design pat-
terns that cover all phases of the design process. Or this may be simply because
the problems encountered in software design are different from those found in
architecture and are not amenable to solution by pattern languages.
    Recently, J obnson has advocated pattern languages to describe how to use
use object-oriented frameworks [16]. Johnson uses a pattern language to explain
how to extend and customUe the Hotdraw drawing editor framework. However,
714       EfI,h Gamma

      these patterns are not design paUema; they are more descriptions of how to
      reuse existing component. and frameworb instead of rules for generating new
      designs.
          eGad', recent paper on object-oriented patterns [6] is &lao motivated by
      Aleza.nder'. work but is more closely related to our work. The paper has seven
      patterns: "Broadcast" i. the aame as Observer, but the other patterns are dif-
      ferent from our•. In general, Coad'. patterns seem to be more c10eely related to
      analysis than design. Design pattern. like Wrapper and Flyweight are unlikely to
      be generated naturally during analyaia unleaa the analyat know. thelle patterns
      well and thinke in terms of them. Coad'. patterD.l could naturally arise from a
      simple attempt to model & problem. In fact, it is hard to see how any large model
      could avoid using patterns like "State Acroee a Collection" (which explains how
      to use aggregation) or "Behavior Acro.. a Collection" (which describes how to
      distribute responsibility amoDg objects in an aggregate). The patterns in OUl'
      catalog are typical of a mature object-oriented design, one that hal departed
      from the o.rigin.a l analysis model in an attempt to make a system of reusable
      objects. In practice, both types of patterns are probably useful.


      6    Conclusion

      Design patterns have revolutionised the way we think about, design, and teach
      object-oriented sy,tem•• We have found them applicable in many stages of the
      design process-initial design, reusc, refactoring. They have given us a new level
      of abstraction for system design.
          New levels of abstraction often afford opportunities for increased automa-
      tion. We are investigating how interactive tools can take advantage of design
      patterns. One of these tools lets a user explore the space of objects in a running
      program and watch their interaction. Througb observation the user may discove.r
      existing or entirely new patterns; the tool leta the user record and catalog his
      observations. The user may thus gain a better understanding of the application,
      the libraries on which it is based, and design in general.
          Design patterns may have an even more profound impact on how object-
      oriented eystema are designed than we have discuased. Common to most patterns
      is that they permit certain aspecte of a eystem to he varied independently. This
      leads to thinking about design in terms of "Wbat aspect of a design should be
      variable?" Answers to true question lead to certain applicable design patterns,
      and their application leads subsequently to modification of a design. We refer to
      this design activity as variation-oriented deaigJ.l and discU88 it more fuUy in
      the catalog of patterns (12].
          But some caveats are in order. Design patterns should not be applied in-
      discriminately. They typically achieve flexibility and variability by introducing
      additional levels of indirection and can therefore complicate a design. A design
      pattern should only be applied when the lle.xibility it affords is actually needed.
      The consequences described in a pattern help determine this. Moreover, one is
                                                          Original HIstoric Documents      71 5

often temp\ecl to brand any new programming trick a new design pattern. A true
design pattern will be non-trivial and will have had more than one application.
    We hope that the deaip patterns described in this paper and in the compan-
ion catalog will provide the object-oriented community both a common design
terminology and a repertoire of reusable deaigna. Moreover, we hope the catalog
will motivate othera to deac:ribe their systems in terms of design patterns and
develop their own design patterna for othera to reuse.

       Conseq uences
          Using Wrappers to add properties is more flexible than using inheritance. With
          Wrappers, properties can be aUached and detached at run-time lIimply by chang-
          ing the Wrapper. Inheritance would require creating a new dUll Cor each property

          clutters the name lip ace of clUlles unnecessarily and IIhould be avoided. Moreover.
          providing different Wrapper danell for a IIpecific Component clull allows mixing
          and matching behaviors and properties.
       Examples

          bellishments to widgets. Examples include InterViews [22). ET++ [31]. and the
          ParcPla.ce Smalltalk dan library [28]. More exotic application. of Wrappers are
          the DebuggingGlyph from InterViews and the PassivityWrapper from ParcPla.ce
